Laboratory observations of the Hairyback (Aspidiophorus polystictos) at a constant 20 °C [T = 20 °C] revealed that the age at birth, defined as the moment of hatching from the egg, occurs approximately 2 days [ab = approximately 2 days] after oviposition. This rapid developmental timeline places the species among the faster-maturing members of the Chaetonotidae, likely an adaptation to exploiting transient microhabitats rich in bacterial and algal films. Newly hatched individuals, or neonates, emerge at a total length at birth of roughly 0.0090 cm [Lb = roughly 0.0090 cm], a diminutive size that necessitates immediate onset of feeding on interstitial microbial communities. The wet weight at birth of these neonates was measured at 2.38 × 10⁻⁸ g [Wwb = 2.38 × 10⁻⁸ g], reflecting their minimal investment in yolk reserves relative to some other meiofaunal gastrotrichs. This low initial mass is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes early exogenous feeding and rapid juvenile growth over prolonged maternal provisioning.

As the juvenile undergoes its period of rapid mass gain, its size increases markedly by the fifth day of life. At 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the total length at 5 days reaches approximately 0.0122 cm , representing a substantial proportional increase from birth dimensions. This growth trajectory is fueled by continuous grazing on bacteria and detrital particles within the sediment matrix. The ultimate total length of a fully grown, reproductively viable organism in this species has been recorded as 0.0136 cm [Li = 0.0136 cm]. This adult size is notably modest even by gastrotrich standards, a trait that facilitates occupation of the thinnest water films and interstitial spaces between sand grains. The relatively small asymptotic length likely imposes constraints on fecundity relative to larger-bodied congeners, a trade-off that must be compensated by other life-history parameters.

Sexual maturation in Aspidiophorus polystictos proceeds rapidly under the standard thermal regime of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. The time since birth at puberty, marking the onset of gametogenesis and the development of functional reproductive organs, was measured as 4.2 days [tp = 4.2 days]. at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]This extremely abbreviated juvenile period is characteristic of opportunistic, r-selected meiofauna occupying ephemeral aquatic microhabitats where early reproduction confers a significant fitness advantage by reducing the risk of pre-reproductive mortality. Upon reaching this developmental milestone, young individuals quickly transition into the reproductively active adult stage. The onset of reproductive activity is thus synchronized with the attainment of near-ultimate body size, ensuring that energy resources can be partitioned between somatic maintenance and the demands of offspring production.

During the reproductively active phase, which can span a considerable portion of the adult lifespan, female Hairybacks achieve a maximum daily output of roughly 0.52 offspring per day when maintained at 20 °C [Ri = roughly 0.52 offspring per day when maintained at 20 °C]. This peak reproductive rate, derived from the ratio of clutch size to inter-clutch interval, underscores a strategy of moderate, sustained fecundity rather than a single, massive reproductive bout. The ultimate wet weight of a sexually mature adult, measured at 8.05 × 10⁻⁸ g [Wwi = 8.05 × 10⁻⁸ g], represents a more than threefold increase over the birth mass. This adult body mass provides the physiological capacity to support continuous egg production, although the energetic demands of reproduction are considerable for an organism of this size. Fecundity is thus intimately tied to the individual's nutritional state and the quality of its microalgal food resources.

The complete life cycle of Aspidiophorus polystictos is remarkably compressed. The maximum lifespan recorded under controlled laboratory conditions at 20 °C [T = 20 °C] was 24.6 days [am = 24.6 days], indicating that the entire progression from zygote to senescent death is completed in less than one month. Such brevity of life is typical for many gastrotrich species, driven by high metabolic rates and the pressures of living in unpredictable, often desiccating, freshwater environments. Following the post-reproductive period, natural mortality ensues through progressive physiological deterioration rather than catastrophic events. The species' life history is therefore characterized by a rapid pace-of-life syndrome: early maturation at the expense of larger body size, continuous reproduction over a short lifespan, and minimal parental investment, all of which are finely tuned to the demands of a transient interstitial existence.
